en: The *Bṛhatī*: A Commentary on the *Śābarabhāṣya*
The first quarter of the sixth chapter.
When substances are connected with an action, they are related as subordinate factors (guṇa). 1.1.1.

Now, why is the statement of the connection (*saṃbandha*) not made here by means of the *vṛtti*? We reply: because there is no connection. For the qualification (*adhikāra*) depends upon the five characteristics (*pañcalakṣaṇa*). [Since it depends on the five characteristics, there is a need for them. If that is so, then all five must be mentioned. No.
[These are] to be proclaimed. Furthermore, there exists no such thing as a "collection" (*samudāya*) that is a distinct entity.
If there is no connection even with the five [factors], how then is it said that "the section (*adhikāra*) depends upon the five characteristics"?

When the five [factors] have been completed as mutually dependent, there is the occasion for the *adhikāra* (the governing topic); for it is said that the *adhikāra* depends upon the five characteristics (*pañcalakṣaṇa*), and not merely from the perspective of cause. The instruction does not extend beyond the sequence.

This is the reason for the objection. Rather, the inquiry is whether or not there exists any qualified person (*adhikārī*) when the instruction extends to the sequence [of actions]. Is there an instruction even for one who lacks qualification? Certainly there is, in cases such as "Devadatta cooks rice in a pot with firewood," where the objects of the statement are matters already known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nothing further is enjoined therein, precisely because its object has already been established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For it is merely a statement of the essential nature and the capacity of that which has already been apprehended through another definition.
The establishment of the instruction [of substances and so forth] occurs through references to the present by virtue of the need for their meaning;
however, the distinction here is that the knowledge of capacity arises from the instruction itself. Therefore, there is no denotation of a relation.
Furthermore, what is the reason that only one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) is cited as an example, and not those desiring a village (*grāmakāma*) and the like?
Or rather, should every [instance] be cited? For the purpose of establishing the logical principle (*nyāya*), only one example should be cited. It is said in reply:

This is indeed true; however, in this context, the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) establishes the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the final position (*uttara-pakṣa*) by means of defining that which is denoted by the word "heaven" (*svarga*). And this [definition] is not possible in cases such as "one desiring a village" (*grāma-kāma*) and so forth, because even when the pleasure has ceased, [the desire for the village remains].
Because of the employment of the word "village" (*grāma*). Therefore, in cases such as "one who desires a village," either a different locus (*adhikaraṇa*) must be stated,
or it must be said that there is a denotation of a means (*sādhana*), because words such as "village" (when followed by "desire") denote a substance (*dravya*).

To this it is replied: all [examples] indeed should have been cited; however, the term *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven) was cited merely for the sake of illustration. Now, it was argued that the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and final (*uttara-pakṣa*) positions based on the naming of that which is desired do not apply to cases such as "one desiring a village" (*grāmakāma*). That statement is incorrect. How is it incorrect? It is incorrect in this way: [text continues].

It has been stated that the word "svarga" (heaven) refers to things desired by virtue of being objects of desire; this should be understood to apply to "those desiring a village" (*grāmakāma*) and so forth as well. For that which is not desired cannot be associated with the act of desiring.
Therefore, even if one accepts that the word *svarga* denotes a place, because it is still connected with desire, [it must denote] pleasure (*prīti*).

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position was established on the grounds that this word "heaven" (svarga) denotes a substance (dravya). In the final conclusion (rāddhānta), however, since desire does not proceed in the absence of pleasure, he has demonstrated that the usage refers exclusively to pleasure.

The word "heaven" (*svarga*) has not, however, been refuted as being a location. In the same way, those such as "one who desires a village" (*grāmakāma*) are also employed by virtue of being objects of pleasure; it is not said that they are [employed] by virtue of being means. For this very reason, having proposed the alternatives "is heaven the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) or is the sacrifice?", it was stated that "desire (*kāma*) is the goal to be accomplished. What is meant by this is: what is the object of desire?

Is the word "heaven" (svarga) employed as a qualifier of the agent by virtue of being desired, such that the object of desire becomes a subordinate element? But surely, in the expression "one who desires heaven" (svargakāma), desire itself is perceived as being merely subordinate.

This very point is investigated here: is the relationship [of the word] according to its denotation (*abhidhāna*), or is the denotation according to the application (*viniyoga*)? If the denotation were according to the application, would this not be a *bahuvrīhi* compound? Who has said that this is not a *bahuvrīhi*? If it is a *bahuvrīhi*, then [the suffix -ya] is a secondary member (*upasarjana*); thus, "kāma" becomes "kāmya."
Because it has another word-meaning as its primary referent. For this very reason, its connection with the number of the agent— pertaining to that which has already been commenced—
is understood from the statement, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice."
"Those desiring prosperity should sacrifice.
This being the case, a doubt is untenable; nor is there a traditional rule (smaraṇa) that the *bahuvrīhi* compound may be used by the Blessed One Pāṇini even for his own sake.
[Objection: It is said: We too do not say that the *bahuvrīhi* compound has its own meaning (*svārtha*) alone;
rather, is this *bahuvrīhi* for the sake of another (*parārtha*), or is it for its own sake? Furthermore, how is it for the sake of another, or how is it for its own sake?

That which has an established meaning (*siddhārtha*) is for the sake of another; whereas if its meaning is something yet to be accomplished (*sādhyārtha*), then it is for its own sake. In this regard, now—
We do not know whether the *siddhārtha* (the established meaning) is presented for the sake of another (*parārthatayā*), or whether it is presented as something to be accomplished (*sādhyatayā*).

[Objection: Is it not a contradiction that it be both the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) and the meaning to be accomplished (*sādhyārtha*)? [Response: There is no contradiction here, because even that which is to be accomplished is indeed for the sake of another. And it has been said: "And the fruit [is a subsidiary], because it exists for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatvāt*)."
Thus, the doubt is indeed justified.
But even so, it may be argued that such a doubt is not tenable, because this is understood as a qualification of the agent (*kartṛviśeṣaṇa*) [as indicated by the suffix of the] verb (*ākhyāta*).

Because of the connection with the number of the agent [expressed by] the past participle; and the venerable Pāṇini records that number as belonging to the agent of that verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Furthermore, when heaven is the goal to be accomplished—that is, for the attainment of heaven—the one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) possesses the status of agent, not for the accomplishment of the sacrifice. Nor does a connection with the number residing in another verbal suffix occur for one who is occupied elsewhere.

Just as [the word] *pacati* [is understood from] *pathataḥ*, here too the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) of "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*) is understood. Why is this *bahuvrīhi* compound [in *svargakāmaḥ*] one whose meaning is already established (*siddhārtha*), and not one whose meaning is something to be accomplished (*sādhyārtha*)? This alone is appropriate here; for it was stated in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* that there is no such thing as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) whose meaning is something to be accomplished. Therefore, the sacrifice—

In this context, it is precisely the duty (*kartavyatā*) of that very [sacrifice] which is determined, because the word *yajati* (he sacrifices) denotes an action (*bhāvārtha*). Nor is there a lack of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between the word expressing the goal and the sacrifice; for if there is such unity, then within that single sentence—
There is no comprehension of two distinct things to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Now, one might object: "Just as in the case of the injunction 'He sprinkles the rice-grains' (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), where there is syntactic unity with the sprinkling—which is itself the means—regarding the *sādhya* residing in the rice-grains (the object of the rite), so too shall it be here. Do not speak thus. For in that case, indeed...

In that case, rice grains, being connected [as objects], become recipients of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) by virtue of being *kārakas*. Here, however, the relationship between the sacrifice and heaven as action and *kāraka* is not established through anything else; nor is it determined in this very context, as in the case of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
Why? Because even that which is to be produced may have a connection with a *kāraka*. If it does so, let it be so.
There is no connection with an agent for that which is already produced. How then is it said, "he cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*)?

The meaning is that he makes the post connected with the act of cutting. Because it is something not previously known in the world, it is called a "sacrificial post" as defined by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*).

And as for the statement that the connection [with the action] is "extraordinary" (*alaukika*), what does this mean? It means that it is extraordinary by virtue of being denoted by the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post), and not by virtue of its connection with the act of cutting (*chidi*). Therefore, even here, something is produced by the cutting of the *khadira* wood and other materials which serve as the *kāraka* (instrumental factor). However, in the case of heaven (*svarga*), its status as a *kāraka* with respect to the meaning of the sacrifice (*yajya*) is indeed extraordinary.

[The opponent replies: "Just as in the case of 'he sprinkles the rice-grains' (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), a relationship [of agent and object] is not possible here in the injunction 'one desiring heaven should sacrifice' (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*).

Nor does one who knows the words (the grammarian) remember any other relationship; or, if he were to remember one, he would be contradicted due to the lack of authoritative evidence. Therefore, the gods will cause doubt in this matter."

To this it is replied: this might be so if the relationship were indeed cognizable through only the four means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And it has been stated that "the authority of the word [of scripture] exists because of its independence"; this was rightly said, for that very [independence]— [...is what establishes its authority. (p. 012)

Otherwise, it fails. How so? Because the establishment of the subject matter (*adhikāra*) depends on the establishment of the application (*prayoga*), and the establishment of the application depends on the establishment of the instruction (*upadeśa*).

If this is the case, then this would simply become a definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*); yet there is indeed another definition of the means of valid cognition as well, because the subject matter is supplementary to the fivefold definition.

How, then, is this defined as a different characteristic? It is defined as follows: although the introduction of the subject matter (*adhikāra*) was already resolved within the first definition by means of the challenge to its validity (*pramāṇākṣepa*), it is now investigated whether that very same subject matter is actually tenable or not. Nor is the challenge to the subject matter based solely on invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). How, then, is it so?
Because the connection with the qualification (*adhikāra*) is not understood. But surely, even such non-understanding constitutes a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*). True, it is so;

however, there is a lack of authority regarding the qualification, but not regarding the mere meaning of the word. Furthermore, in the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), the word does not [fail to convey] its meaning...
The sense that [the word] "touches" has been refuted. Therefore, the designation of other characteristics is established.

Consequently, it has been stated that the comprehension of the effect arises from the five characteristics, but not that "this is its effect. And in the absence of this comprehension, even if there were a comprehension of the mere effect, it would not be so, because of the lack of performance.

But was it not stated in the fourth [chapter] that even in the absence of a qualification (*adhikāra*), a postulation of a fruit is taught, namely: "That [act] would be for the sake of heaven"? True, it was so stated. However, when a qualification is possible, that [postulation of a fruit] is based precisely on that qualification;
it has been stated that a qualification exists even when it is not explicitly heard in the text. But when a qualification is impossible, for what unmentioned thing could there be a postulation?
Therefore, the qualification must be stated.
Now, it may be objected that certain venerable grammarians consider the agent alone to be the qualified subject.

Those who maintain that "he who is understood as the agent in a particular action is the one authorized therein" hold that what is called "authorization" (*adhikāra*) is not some distinct entity; rather, they consider it to be the connection with an action. Furthermore, they believe that the Brāhmaṇas and others are understood as agents by virtue of the Smṛti: "Study, sacrifice, and the giving of gifts [are for] the twice-born."
Furthermore, the attribution of the fruit to the agents is understood through such indicators as the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) and so forth; this indeed is the position of Bādari.
He considers that the connection is established with substances, qualities, and purificatory acts (*dravya-guṇa-saṃskāra*), and not with the sacrifice, the fruit, and the person.
In this way, the connection with the action will be logically consistent; otherwise, for one who is qualified [for the rite], the action—

The connection [of these words with the verb] is difficult to establish; therefore, words such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) are merely qualifiers of the agent, just like the expression "he offers in a broken vessel."
But if this were the case, would it not follow that there is no entry of another agent? Let it be so that there is no such entry;

nevertheless, it cannot be said that the postulation of the cognition of a relationship is impossible. Furthermore, it will be established by the scriptural statement itself, and for this very reason, the case-ending denoting an agent does not arise. Since the number is expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the nominative case is used.

And this is its origin. Otherwise, one would have to seek another case-ending for the qualified person (*adhikārī*), or there would have to be a genitive denoting the residual relation (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇā*), as in "one should sacrifice for the sake of one desiring heaven" (*yajeta svargakāmasya*). Furthermore, that this is a designation of the agent is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), as in "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*) and "heaven is sacrificed for by one desiring it" (*ijyate svargakāmena*). Otherwise, indeed...

Even if the word is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva-sādhana*), the instrumental case would not apply to *svargakāma* because it is not a factor of action (*akāraka*). As for what was further stated—that an action becomes fruitless and that people do not engage in what is fruitless—to that we reply:
Because of the inherent nature of karma, it will produce something; and that [production] occurs for the sake of prosperity even in your own view, as in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*).
The performance of action arises solely from the understanding of its duty (*kartavyatā*), and not from a connection with a fruit. As for the fruit—

For if there were a relationship [between the Veda and its meaning], it would follow that [the meaning] is to be understood through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, the established reason—that [the Veda] is independent—would be undermined, because it would entail the consequence of dependence. Therefore, since [the Veda] states "the ritual act must be performed by agents," it lacks authoritative status (*anadhikāra*).

It is said: This prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not the best, for we shall explain later on how, in this view, the word "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*) does not connect [with the action]. If that is so, then how does the doubt arise—whether it is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) that is taught as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), or rather the desire (*kāma*)? But surely, if the meaning of the verbal root were the object to be accomplished, the word "desire" [would be redundant].

It has been stated that otherwise [the injunction] would not be connected [to the context]. It is not the case that it is not connected; rather, by virtue of being a subordinate element (*aṅga*), it follows that one must perform the mental meditation, just as in the case of the injunction: "One should meditate upon the ocean with the mind."

[Objection: If this is so, then it would follow that both [the sacrifice and the result] are stated as things to be performed. [Reply: No; while it is true that both are stated, it is the relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*) between them that is being considered here. [Objection: How then is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) established on the basis that the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) has an accomplished entity as its meaning? [Reply: Even the prima facie view holds that it has a goal to be achieved (*sādhya*) as its meaning. [Objection: How then is an already existing thing (*bhūta*) taught for the sake of something yet to be brought into being (*bhavya*)?

Thus he says: this is not a fault, for here only an existing reality (bhūta) is taught. And if it were not already established by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), it would be taught for the sake of establishing its material cause. But in the case of an instruction, it is indeed an existing reality. And for this very reason, in the eleventh [book]...

That which is the locus [of the discussion] is also non-redundant according to logic. This being the case regarding the subject matter, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) has argued for the prima facie position that "the existent is for the sake of the yet-to-be-existent" (*bhūtam bhavyāya*), supported by the arguments stated in the scriptures.
Furthermore, this other point is now considered: how so? Does the word "heaven" (*svarga*) denote pleasure (*prīti*), or does it denote a substance (*dravya*)?

Regarding the word "utterance" (*vacana*): likewise, the introduction of [the girl] being eight or sixteen years old, the denial of the location, and the admission [of the act] are not at all useful. Now, was it not said by us: "Is the word 'heaven' (*svarga*) employed as having desire for its object, or as referring to a substance? If that is so, what is the purpose of denying the location? [The answer is: the establishment of the means of proof (*sādhanasiddhi*).

That region, it is said, cannot be perceived by those who are still living; and for that which is unperceived, the status of being a subordinate material cause—like that of the ocean—is impossible. Therefore, even if the existence of a location were admitted, the mention of "two years," "eight years," and so forth, is quite appropriate.
Even though [it might seem so] from the mere hearing of "pure bliss," nevertheless our position is not undermined; thus, this statement is indeed for the purpose of establishing our own thesis.

Since practical activity (*vyavahāra*) cannot be established through a mere general understanding, the conclusion is that only the status of being a means to pleasure (*sukhasādhanatvamātra*) is accepted.
Therefore, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers the injunction to refer to the sacrifice itself. And for this very reason...
Thus it is established that "words denoting action have being as their meaning; from them, the action is to be understood.
Otherwise, a contradiction would indeed arise.

But surely, on this view, whatever that may be will simply be so; for the fruit of an action is never perceived as having a non-agent as its substratum. But surely, in cases such as "one sacrifices the Soma," there are indeed agents—
We do not perceive [such a result]. Therefore, this is improper, because the primacy of the aforementioned deity has been refuted in the ninth [book].
Now, it might be argued that for one whose human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) is not yet known, a refinement (*saṃskāra*)—whether direct or indirect—is not possible.
Thus it was stated in the section concerning *saktu*. Furthermore, the deity has not been made known by anyone as being for the sake of human beings in any manner whatsoever.

[Objection: But is it not well-known that deities protect human beings? [Response: It has already been stated in the ninth [chapter] that such a notion is like a yakṣa in a banyan tree, because it lacks any foundation and is therefore not to be respected.
But surely, the instruction regarding the sacrifice ought to be authoritative for this well-known fact, just as it is for the [location of] the country.

This must necessarily be accepted even for the sake of what is eternal. This is not tenable; for the instruction is authoritative only to the extent that "one should perform the sacrifice," and not that "the sacrifice is beneficial to the person."

[Page 021] But surely, since there is an absence of actual performance, even so let the instruction exist; yet it has been stated that it is not so, for no one engages in an action that provides no benefit. But has this not also been stated: "Because of the comprehension of what ought to be done"?

[It must be] set in motion, not because of the understanding of a benefit, for that would entail the consequence of dependence. And thus, even though this [agent] is eternally obstructed, it is indeed non-obstructive. If this is so, let all this—the eternal performance as well as the fruit—be such; nevertheless, our position is established. Therefore, desire is not the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), since it is already existent (*bhūta*).
Because it is understood from that [text]. How then do the ritualists (yājñika) teach them as distinct, saying "the optional" and "the obligatory"?
This teaching must be incorrect because it lacks a foundation.
If this is so, then it follows that the entitlement belongs solely to the agent; and yet, the [notion of] the agent has already been refuted.

In that designation, the term "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*) is not connected. True, the status of being a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) without a substrate has been refuted; however, its status as a subordinate element with a substrate remains.

It is indeed established, because it is designated as a quality (*guṇa*). But what is the distinction between these two? It has been stated that one has a material cause (*sopādānatva*) and the other lacks a material cause (*nirupādānatva*). True, it has been stated; however, I ask about the distinction in terms of cognition (*pratīti*). If, in cognition, there is a distinction arising from the attainment of a relation (*saṃbandha*), then why state a further distinction [regarding the cause]? True, if there were no distinction...

It has been stated that the relationship of dependence (*apekṣā-sambandha*) is understood when there is a substratum (*sattva*), but it is not understood when there is no such substratum. Therefore, what is called "authorization" (*adhikāra*) does not exist as something distinct from the agent (*kartṛ*). Or else, a specific distinction must be stated.
But surely, as has been shown, the instigation (*pravṛtti*) of one who is about to act is produced by the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc.)?

In the *Nirukta*, it says: "Do! Do! For this very reason, there is also the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "He [the ignorant person] knows 'this must be done by me,' but he does not know the means. And it has been shown that they recite: "One seeking to practice sorcery (*abhicāra*) should sacrifice."

"One should perform the malevolent rite" (abhicaritavyam). First of all, it cannot be said that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth denote the activity of one who is already engaged in activity, because such a definition is not heard in the grammatical treatises, and because there are deviations in actual usage. As for the definition: [text continues]

He does not specify whether it concerns one who is already acting or one who is not. Furthermore, the employment [of verbal suffixes] is observed only in cases such as commands (*ājñā*) where [the person] has not yet acted. But surely, optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth occur only for one who has understood the command? No; the employment is not for the sake of impelling one who is already acting, because there is deviation in cases such as invitations (*āmantraṇa*). Even in the case of a command, it is the impelling of one who has not yet acted.

In this way, activity is induced for one who was previously not engaged in a particular application; nor is activity understood from the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth in a general sense, because they are restricted to specific [meanings]. Furthermore, it has been stated in the *tadbhūtādhikaraṇa* that words denote [their meanings] as already connected (*anvitābhidhāna*). As for what was further said—that when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is produced, it shows [the agent] as "doing, doing" (*kurukuru*)—[that too is explained by the above].

The meaning of a word cannot be understood from mere usage alone; for it has been stated that the perception of a relation established by no other means is the cause for determining the meaning of a word, and that an unerring cause is desired by those who possess knowledge of causes.

But if this is so, then the application of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers would also be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Therefore, the cause for the fixed relationship between word and meaning must be stated. This is what is said: the optative suffixes and others do not deviate from "incitement" (*pravartana*), because it is understood in all cases. And when there is incitement—[in the case where the causative suffix *ṇic* arises] even when [the agent] has not yet acted.

And because [it occurs] at the beginning of commands and so forth, it can be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the meaning of a word consists in just that much.
As for the [notions] "this is indeed ordained by the Veda" or "this must be done by me,"...

And as for the statement, “One seeking [success through] sorcery should sacrifice,” that was shown when it is established that there is a distinct qualification (adhikāra) connected with desire; it was stated there with the intention of expressing what is already established and what is not yet established. But here, it is said that there is no such distinct [qualification]. Therefore, that [previous example] is not [analogous]. If...

Furthermore, this instruction is intended precisely for one who is already engaged in activity; at that time, the very purpose of the instruction is lost, because the sentence is directed toward the fact that "this is the means for that. And it has already been stated that there is no verbal authority (*śābda-pramāṇa*) regarding the actual nature of the means itself.

What then? It is precisely in the performance [of the act]. Therefore, it is logical that the purpose of the instruction is to incite one who has not yet begun to act. For this very reason, those learned in the science of words consider that the causal suffix (*ṇic*) expresses the motive for one who is already acting, whereas the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. express the motive for one who has not yet begun to act. Consequently, the cognition of what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*) alone is the cause of performance, and not—

There is a desire for the fruit. And so, in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, having stated "one should perform," it was explained that because of its connection with the term "desirous of heaven" (*svargakāma*), the meaning is "one should bring about heaven" (*svargaṃ bhāvayet*), and not that "the desirous of heaven should perform heaven. This must necessarily be understood in this way; otherwise, there would be no qualification (*anadhikāra*) for those [injunctions] such as "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), since [heaven] would not be the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Because there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
But if this is so, does it not follow that the connection with the members [of dependent origination] is not established? It is not established that there is a connection with the members, if...

The Śruti and other means of knowledge are not invalid; nor is their authority dependent upon being employed for some other purpose. This is because they contain instructions on the subsidiaries even for eternal rites. And if [the result] does not accrue, what can we do? We have already stated that the Prayājas and other such elements must indeed be performed separately. As for those restrictive rules (niyamas) which have visible purposes—
They are not taught as being without a constituent part even when there is an agent's entitlement; therefore, the instruction pertains only to the meaning of the verbal root, not to desire.
If people do not engage in what is fruitless, how then [is there engagement] in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), even though their status as duties is understood?

They are to be instructed. Furthermore, what punishment do those who fail to engage in action deserve, even when the result is available? Therefore, the very understanding of engagement is the cause of engagement. In that regard, those who do not engage abandon the scripture and do not perform what ought to be done;
however, those who possess desire, even while engaging in fruitful actions, do not abandon the scripture.
Nor do they fail to perform what ought to be performed; therefore, on this view, there is all the more non-implementation of the scripture.
But surely, on the view that the agent possesses the entitlement, the injunction (*niyoga*) is purposeless, for the agent is already engaged in activity.

Or rather, one receives the designation of a "factor" (*kāraka*) because one will cause those already engaged to engage. In that regard, as for the Brāhmaṇas and others in relation to sacrifices and so forth, they receive the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) on the grounds that they have been engaged; or perhaps they are being engaged; or else they will be caused to engage.
In no way is this tenable. If, first of all, they have already been engaged, what [is there left to do]?

The mandate (*niyoga*) will bring it about. Or, even if they are currently active, it is still useless. Or, if the intention is that they "will cause [them] to act," from where does this cognition come prior to the mandate? If you say, "It will arise from the mandate itself," then the mandate would not belong to the agent; rather, agency would result only for one who is already connected to the mandate. Therefore...
The agency of an agent is difficult to maintain. But if this were so, would it not follow that the connection with all the *kārakas* (factors of action) is denied?

And what would an injunction (*niyoga*) accomplish in actions devoid of *kārakas*? If it is argued that the injunction will apply once the entire collection of *kārakas* is understood as being to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*), then the same applies to the agent as well. Thus...

However, because the scripture is the instigator [of action], even one who possesses desire engages [in it]; thus, the accomplishment of performance is established. This being the case, an objection is raised: "An action whose agent is a specific person must be performed by that very agent alone"—this is the intended connection with the thought that [the agent] will act.
Success! Therefore, even within the context of the agent (*kartṛ*), there is no fault. Moreover, this must necessarily be accepted:

that the meaning [of the suffix] is the connection with other factors of action (*kāraka*). For even for those [factors], no connection is understood from anything other than the accomplishment of the mandate (*niyoga*). Therefore, it must be accepted that prior to the mandate, there is either no connection at all [between the factors].
Therefore, the prior comprehension of the relationship is caused by that very [usage], or else the established authority of the word must be rescinded.
Now, [one might object]: "In the case of kingship and so forth, one is first authorized [with the words] 'O Sir, you are entitled to this [office] performed in such a manner'."

From the act, the relationship between action and its factors (kriyākāraka) is observed. In what sense does it have an agent? It is appropriate in cases such as kingdoms and the like, because one observes the presence of agents possessing those qualities among other persons even when [the kingdom] has passed away. But here, however, [this is] without a mandate (niyoga).

Nor can it be said that there is another person [as the author], because all activity is preceded by that [the Veda]. Furthermore, in the case of treatises on statecraft (*daṇḍanīti*) and the like, since the instruction is preceded by other systems of philosophy (*darśana*), it might be possible for a specific person who has experienced [the truth] to have authority over them. Even in those cases, however, it is merely a statement regarding what is worthy (*arha*); thus, there is no authority of an author.

Thus, agency does not arise from [mere] entitlement (*adhikāra*). And it is established that, within the context of agency, the state of "desiring heaven" is a qualification of the agent, not a qualification of the fruit. Consequently, everything must be performed by everyone. Accordingly, this instruction on knowledge is for all, because through the performance of everything, there is the attainment of the whole.
Thus, all this has been stated: that Brahman, which is everything, is taught through the method of instruction, both in terms of knowledge and in terms of practice.
For this very reason, there is the following exclamation from those who maintain the existence of an agent and a qualified performer: "On the path of untruth..."
Having remained [in that state], one should then manifest the Truth.
He considers this to be the rule for all teachings and for all performances of every duty: "These desires are true, but they have untruth as their covering."

Thus says the Śruti. The intended meaning is that instruction given part by part is false; furthermore, differentiation is based on passion and the like. Therefore, because of the observation of the section concerning the factors of action (kāraka), there is the observation of another meaning.

This is delusion. For this very reason, the authors of the *Dharmaśāstras* declare, "To have desire as one's essence is not praiseworthy," considering the attainment of results through non-Vedic means. Indeed, they consider that the study of the Vedas and the application of ritual action (*karmayoga*) are for the sake of desire; thus, they maintain their application toward knowledge and action [respectively]. "All this, indeed, is Brahman."
The statement of the Brāhmaṇa, “One should meditate upon this very one as ‘tajjalān,’ which is peaceful,” illuminates this very position.

For when that which is desired is being taught, it does not become something achievable by every agent; because desire is seen to be distinct [in each case], the oneness of all is therefore not established. Consequently, [passages such as] "The Person alone is all this," and so forth...

The explanatory passages (arthavāda) of the mantras would not be untenable; as for the doctrines of difference, it has already been resolved that the instruction is indeed partial and based upon that [difference]. But if there were ultimate non-difference, what would unity be based upon? For this very reason, the venerable Pāṇini, in the case of roots such as *pac* (to cook), [teaches] apart from the distinction between action and its factors (kāraka).

The author of the *Smṛti* does not record that there is a distinct action called "the person to be enjoined" (*niyojya*) within the sense of the term *niyoga*. Now, one might object: "But isn't the root *yuj* also listed among the roots beginning with *pac*?
True, it is so listed; however, the *Smṛti* does not record that the agent of sacrifices and other rites is the object (*karman*) of the root *yuj*.

But has this not been stated by you yourself: "For the agent is enjoined"? What is meant by this is that the agent in sacrifices and the like is the object (*karman*) of the root *yuj* (to enjoin). If it is said that the means (*sādhana*) of the root *yuj* is what is enjoined, then our position is established. What then? Does the venerable Pāṇini not remember this?

This was stated with the intention of [showing] that it is not a *kāraka* (an agentive factor). In that context, when desire (*kāma*) is the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*), there is the status of being a *kāraka* due to the injunction (*niyoga*).

To say "the injunction is the agency" (*kartṛtva*) is a shift to a different meaning (*arthāntarāpatti*). And it has been stated that in such a shift of meaning, there is no perceived praise (*stuti*). Thus, this praising of the fruit for those who possess desire is like the binding of a crane in the sky.
It has been stated that for those possessed by desire, there is delusion (*moha*).

Therefore, the wise have declared that the qualification for action belongs to the agent, according to the principle: "That which has already come into being is taught for the sake of that which is yet to be.

For this very reason, even the distinction between verbal roots (*ākhyāta*)—that is, the definition of their difference—is not applicable [in this context], as there is no primary action (*guṇakarma*) whatsoever.

[The opponent says: "Something is a primary action (*pradhānakarman*). [The author replies: But if the goal were optional (*kāmya*), then all verbal suffixes would attain the status of being subordinate (*guṇabhāva*);
consequently, the meaning of the sūtra—"those [actions] are of two kinds"—would be untenable.
[The opponent objects: "But that [sūtra] will have the obligatory (*nitya*) in mind. [The author replies: It does not have the obligatory in mind; for even there...
The reason is that we observe the attainment of a different state; for those by whom a substance (*dravya*) is intended to be produced, it follows that it remains merely a quality (*guṇa*).

In our view, however, since the instruction is directed toward the substance, there is the status of being a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*), and the word "is intended to be produced" refers to the instruction.
This is indeed the case; for it is well said that when instruction is focused on action, the primary importance lies therein.

To this, it is replied: (one's own) name becomes a qualifier of the agent only when, by virtue of being a qualifier, a *kāraka* (case-role) is applicable. However, in this instance, regarding "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), once the pleasure has ceased, that very substance [the desire] no longer exists.

It is that which is denoted by the word "heaven. What follows if this is so? This follows from it: [heaven] is the desired object of desire. What follows from that? A desired thing does not exist for the sake of accomplishing something else; for everything exists for the sake of what is desired. This is what is meant: in a sentence connected with a desired end, the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the other word-meanings is solely for the sake of that [desired end].

It has been stated that "it is the person," and Jaimini [says] that "actions also [are for the sake of the person], because they are for the sake of the fruit"; and since the fruit is for the sake of the person, its very nature as something desired means it is not for the sake of the sacrifice. But was it not said that heaven is what is desired? And that—

"It is a contradiction to say that it is for the sake of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*). It is replied: "Or how could that which is not for the sake of human purpose be desired? In that case, it follows that all this is indeed for the sake of human purpose, and not for the sake of what is merely desired. [True; however, you are wise, long-lived one! For what purpose, then, is the mention of 'the desired' (*iṣṭa*)? Because without the state of being the desired, the status of being for the sake of human purpose is not established.]

Because heaven is indeed desired, its status as a human goal (puruṣārtha) is possible through the scripture; thus, the mention of what is desired is meaningful. This state of being the primary beneficiary (śeṣin) with respect to action—on account of a person's connection to the fruit produced by that action—is called "qualification" (adhikāra). One is said to be "qualified" for that action for whose sake one is engaged in it.

For the word "authorized" (*adhikṛta*) indeed signifies the Lord (the master). For this very reason, even though agency is equal [in both cases], there is the designation of "one who performs the work for the master. But is it not the case that he does not exist at all in the sacrifice? No, certainly not in the sense of the literal meaning of the word; rather, it is in the sense of the scriptural injunction (*śāstrārtha*).

But that is possible; the meanings of the words, however, would be established by implication. Now, it was stated that "the action-words have being as their meaning," and that when desire is the goal to be accomplished, agency in the sacrifice is not logically possible. How, then, is the entitlement established for villages and the like when the word *svarga* (heaven) denotes something desired? It has been said that [this is established] because heaven and so forth are objects of desire.
The mention [of these things] is not for the purpose of qualifying desire.

But surely, positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekau*) are possible only with respect to heaven (*svarga*). We have already stated that positive and negative concomitance are intended merely to demonstrate the object [of desire]. However, it is through their connection with desire that villages and the like are established as objects.
As for the question, "If desire is what is to be accomplished, how can there be agency (*kartṛtva*) in the sacrifice?"—who said that there is agency in the sacrifice?

Rather, there is entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the sacrifice; and agency follows by implication (*arthāt*) for the sake of accomplishing that entitlement. For this very reason, the inclusion of number [in the injunction] occurs.

It is said that the agent’s entitlement [to perform a rite] is based on the intention to sacrifice. Even in the world, one who is authorized for one thing accomplishes another: a minister authorized for the king’s affairs accomplishes his own interests; yet, for the sake of achieving those interests, he possesses the status of an agent within the king’s business.

Furthermore, as for the statement that "words denoting action have being as their meaning," it is said that where there is an injunction (*adhikāra*), the understanding of the fruit arises from those [words]. The meaning is that one should accomplish one's own purpose by means of that instrument (*sādhana*). For this very reason, the status of *udbhid* and other such terms as names (*nāmadheya*) has been stated on account of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*). If so, then what is the meaning of this that was said?
[Page 037] "The state of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*) is not determined from the name alone. By whom was it said that it is otherwise than that?
How then is there the state of being something to be done for desire (*kāma*)? It has been stated: "Because it is understood as something desired (*iṣṭa*). And this must necessarily be so—

This must be accepted. For the accomplishment of performance does not follow merely from the understanding of the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*), as seen in such cases as "Devadatta cooks rice in a pot with firewood. But surely, the understanding of performance will arise from the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth; what then will the qualification (*adhikāra*) accomplish? Of whom [do] the optative suffixes [indicate the duty]?

[They] make known the performance [of the action]. But has it not been stated that [the suffix] is used in the sense of the agent? This is an improper statement, because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence;
thus, the injunction for the agent would be purposeless. For if [the agent were established] from the injunction...

If agency were dependent upon the mandate (*niyoga*), and the mandate upon agency, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Therefore, agency must be understood from the mandate itself; however, the understanding of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) comes from another source, namely, as has been stated, from the connection with a desired end (*iṣṭasaṃbandha*).

If this is so, how is it in the case of "as long as life lasts" (*yāvajjīva*) and similar expressions? Or rather, why would it not apply here? Because life is taught as an established fact (*siddha*). But you yourself have stated that life does not connect as a qualifier of the agent precisely because it is already established. This is incorrect; for it is only an established factor (*siddha*) that connects as a qualifier, and not [an action to be accomplished].

It is the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and not, moreover, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). For it has been stated that the understanding of the result arises from the positive concomitance through verbal testimony, and not that there is a positive concomitance of the possessor of the result, as that would entail the consequence of mutual dependence (*sāpekṣatva*). Therefore, it must be explained how there is entitlement (*adhikāra*) in this case.
This is now stated: in the view that takes the word "as long as" (*yāvat*) in *yāvajjīvam* as a qualification of the agent, the word "as long as" does not enter into positive concomitance.
How so? A lifelong application is not possible; for one who desires a result does not apply himself once the desire for that result has ceased.
Therefore, life must necessarily be sought as the causal condition (*nimitta*). And that [condition] is connected with the person qualified for the rite.

This is not possible in connection with the agent (*kartṛ*). For if there were a connection with the agent, then from the mere statement "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), it would follow that "one must sacrifice as long as one lives"; thus, the impossibility of the word "as long as" (*yāvat*) has already been shown. Furthermore, it has been stated that the status of being an agent cannot be established unless the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is first known prior to the connection with the agent. Even by resorting to another alternative position...

Those learned in the principles of logic maintain that it must be stated that [the Veda] possesses a human purpose (*janavattā*). If that is so, then the qualification for ritual action (*adhikāra*) is not established merely because [the Veda] is accepted as authoritative.

It is not that it is not so; for even if it does not have action as its primary meaning, its capacity [to convey meaning] and its status as a qualification for those entitled to act are established, and thus qualification is proven for both obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites.
Furthermore, as for what was stated— that the status of being an agent is established for [the person] just like other causal factors (kārakas) by virtue of being a means of accomplishment (sādhana),

and that consequently the understanding of the person to be enjoined (niyojya) arises precisely through their connection with an action— this is incorrect, because [in reality] there is no performance...

Even when [the sacrifice] has been produced, its connection with the action is understood, because no other connection exists. Therefore, what has been stated is indeed logical. When one is enjoined toward the object, in the accomplishment of the desired result, the sacrifice is the instrument (*karaṇa*). What word here serves as the basis for this? First of all, the verbal root *yaj* (to sacrifice) denotes merely the sacrifice itself.

Furthermore, it does not [indicate] its connection with anything else. Even the case-ending (*vibhakti*) expresses the agent as the means of accomplishing the action and the number inherent therein; it does not, however, indicate that the sacrifice is for the sake of something else.
The term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) makes known that heaven is what is desired by the person; it does not, however, indicate the primacy of the sacrifice [with respect to that desire].

[Page 041] Whether it be heaven or desire, the nominative case ending has a meaning that is not distinct [from the verb]. However, since terms such as *jyotiṣṭoma* are names (*nāman*), they are dependent on the sacrifice which is being denoted. And the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) does not [denote] the sacrifice...
It has been stated that [the Veda] declares [the sacrifice] as an instrument (*karaṇa*). Therefore, the notion that "one should accomplish heaven by means of the sacrifice" is entirely baseless.

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the mandate (*niyoga*) here: does it enjoin the person toward the desire (*kāma*), or toward the sacrifice? Consequently, there will be an understanding of the mandate alone in one or the other of these two; however, there is no understanding of a mutual relationship between the two.

[Objection: But surely the state of being desired (*iṣṭatva*) is not otherwise possible if the fulfillment of desire does not arise from the sacrifice—[as it was said]. Where has it been seen that this state of being desired does not exist without a means? [Response: It becomes desired precisely because it is desired; if it is argued that "it is understood as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by virtue of its being desired," that is incorrect. By which word is the state of being a goal (*sādhyatā*) expressed?

Only a mere connection with desire is understood regarding heaven, but not whether it is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) or something already established (*siddha*). Therefore, the cause (*nimitta*) by which its status as a causal factor is understood must be stated here. It would be better, then, to let the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) stand.

Therefore, let the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) be a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). Let it be that the one who desires heaven is the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), but not that "one should accomplish heaven by means of sacrifice," because there is no basis for such a causal relation. To this, it is replied: it has already been stated that heaven qualifies the person by virtue of being the object of desire.

And it has also been stated that the injunction (*niyoga*) pertains to the meaning of the verbal root. Thus, this constitutes a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) by virtue of the relationship between the injunction and the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). Indeed, syntactical unity is not possible if there is a lack of correspondence with reality (*ayathārthatva*). Furthermore, the accomplishment of the injunction is the sentence-meaning. In that regard, if the duty to perform the sacrifice itself were [the sole focus], the purpose of the person to be enjoined would not be connected.

Regarding the injunction (*niyoga*): if desire were not connected with the object by means of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), then the comprehension of a single injunction would be undermined. Furthermore, the fault already mentioned applies if the sacrifice were primary. Therefore, the connection to a single injunction occurs precisely through the primacy of desire. This has been stated: "Moreover, he for whom heaven is desired [should perform] the sacrifice..."

To say that one would "bring about" [something] is as if incoherent, for it implies that one desires one thing while doing another. In this context, it can be said that the word itself is the cause (*nimitta*). As for what was stated regarding the demonstration of the non-distinction between the denotation and [the object], that refers to the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of the related).

This has already been answered by [the discussion on] *dhāna*. If that is so, then this was already resolved in the very section concerning "that which has become such" (*tadbhūtādhikaraṇa*); namely, it was resolved that the comprehension of words and word-meanings is indeed unconnected. That section was intended as a counter-position against the theories of mental intuition (*pratibhā*), the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), and the process of inclusion and exclusion (*āvāpoddhāra*); it was not, however, for the purpose of establishing the understanding that words denote only the individual word-meanings.
Therefore, it is logical that one should accomplish heaven by means of sacrifice. [p.
044] What is this [sūtra] "But it is not a means of accomplishment because it exists for that purpose"? This sentence is not a means of accomplishing the meaning of the sentence.

This is what is meant: the sense is that there would not be a sentence that establishes a connection with a single injunction (*ekaniyoga*). Now, it was argued that if one assumes the status of a cause (*nimittatva*), it cannot be said that any single [element] possesses the status of a cause; for this very reason, it is stated "of all" (*sarvasya*). For, in the analysis of words and word-meanings, with respect to each individual word—

It is said that this constitutes the state of being a cause (*nimittabhāva*). Furthermore, it has been stated in that very same place that, regarding the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), everything indeed serves as a cause.

As for what was said—that [the word] "remembers" the expression of the relationship through the connection between the injunction (*niyoga*) and the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*)—that is incorrect;
for it is possible to encompass everything by means of the recollection of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). However, as for the expression itself...

The relationship of relative terms is indeed indefinite, as it is not observed in the case of the Lord (*bhagavat*) in primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), or compounds (*samāsa*). And thus, since the meaning of the sentence serves to establish the injunction, the objection that "activity results from the fruit" is refuted. How so?

In that case, is it the established practice in the *Tantra* that the result (*phala*) is not enjoined? When the sense of the mandate (*niyoga*) has been understood, during the consideration of the occasioning cause (*nimitta*), there arises the conceptualization that "this [result] is obtained from another source, and this too is obtained from that very source"; however, it is not as if something already obtained exists within the meaning of the sentence itself, as was demonstrated in the case of "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*).

Undiscriminating knowledge regarding words and sentences confuses those of dull intellect. There is no such thing as a "word" within a sentence, nor are there any "word-meanings" within a sentence-meaning; for it is only through the comprehension of specific distinctions that [knowledge arises].

The meaning of the sentence [is the primary object], and the sentence is the cause for its comprehension. However, when one postulates the instrumental causes [of that comprehension], there is the designation of "word" and "word-meaning. If this is so, it would follow—just as the proponents of verbal testimony (śābdikas) claim—that the knowledge of words and word-meanings is indeed false. We do not say that their status as instruments is false; rather, [we say they are false] only insofar as they are being comprehended [as the final objects].
In that state, there is non-discrimination regarding the sentence-meaning, and [non-discrimination] regarding the sentence in its capacity as a communicator.
Therefore it has been said: "The cognition of word-meanings arises from words alone, and the cognition of the sentence-meaning arises from the word-meanings";
this is based on the distinction between cause and effect, but not on a distinction in the actual cognition itself. However, by those who follow the verbal [tradition]...

The distinction is that even the *nimitta* (the causal occasion) is negated; this is what is stated in the *Vākyapadīya*. Regarding the existence... [p. 047]: Is the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*) to be expressed as something preceded by a *nimitta* for the root *yaj* (to sacrifice)? There is indeed something to be expressed in its own form (*svarūpataḥ*).

It cannot be said that [the meaning] is denoted by means of a pramāṇa, because the status of being a pramāṇa is understood through its effect (kārya), whereas verbal expression (abhidhāna) resides solely in the individual word-meanings (padārtha). Therefore, it is determined that denotation occurs by means of the optative suffixes (liṅ) and so forth as pramāṇas, and not by means of primary derivatives (kṛt-anta). This is because such usage is observed, and because the comprehension of word-meanings is preceded by linguistic usage. Hence...

The position of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) has also been refuted. If, then, the connection with the object of memory is expressed by the genitive case, how is it that in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*), the nominative case is used? Or rather, there should be a genitive, or else there would be no hearing of any case-ending at all. It is said in reply: this nominative is not dependent upon the mandate (*niyoga*); rather, it is dependent upon the grammatical factor (*kāraka*).

But surely, since the relationship between an action and its factors (kārakas) is preceded by the person to be enjoined (niyojya), that relationship must be expressed by a case-ending associated with that very person. You have spoken truly; however, a case-ending is not possible when the injunction (niyoga) is expressed by the optative suffix (liṅ). For the genitive case depends merely upon a general relationship, and [the injunction] is not such a relationship.

[It is] dependent upon a specific operation (*vyāpāra*). Furthermore, a distinction is understood from the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth. In that case, let there be the accusative case; no, for the operation of the mandate (*niyoga*) has not been expressed. For the accusative occurs when the operation is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*).

The [suffixes] beginning with *ya* [denote] the action (*bhāva*), because the designation of a *kāraka* depends upon the action; and they maintain that what is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) is the action, saying: "The meaning of the root alone, in its pure form, is called 'action' (*bhāva*)."

Therefore, even though the status of being an agent occurs subsequently, it is the cause for the arising of the case-ending here; for the fulfillment of the injunction is accomplished by means of the mere meaning of the nominal stem alone. And for this very reason, when the singularity of the agent has already been expressed, [the suffix is not applied].

The consequence of a second [agent] does not arise; and the presentation of two entities has already been refuted, because no other verbal root (*dhātu*) is employed. Furthermore, the distinction between the subordinate and the principal is based on the intention regarding the grammatical factor (*kāraka*), and this too has already been resolved. For this very reason, the number associated with the agent (*kāmin*) is not the governing factor; rather, only the number associated with the verb (*ākhyāta*) is taken into account.

[Page 050] Then how is it that there is no activity on the part of one who lacks desire? Because the scripture has *niyoga* (the mandate) as its primary purpose, and because desire exists for the sake of accomplishing the object of that *niyoga*. It is not at all suspected that [desire] is a subordinate factor (*aṅga*).

But [the agent] who desires [a result] obtains it. In this matter, it is your lack of discrimination that is at fault. For the relationship of subsidiary and principal (aṅgāṅgibhāva) is not accepted as being dependent on the meaning of the verbal root; rather, even the relationship of subordinate and primary (guṇapradhānabhāva) is stated in the Bhāṣya to be dependent on that very same [root-meaning]. But when the mandate (niyoga) is established, who would not accept that everything is conducive to it? As for the restriction regarding being for the sake of that (tādarthyaniyama):

[This has] been demonstrated. For this very reason, in the section concerning the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*), the author of the Commentary (Śabarasvāmin) showed that the meaning of the sentence consists primarily in the injunction (*niyoga*), by means of such expressions as "one should act" (*kuryāt*). How, then, are these Vedic sentences [to be understood]: "These true desires have falsehood as their covering," "All this, indeed, is Brahman," and so forth? It has been stated:
[The opponent claims:
"There is the comprehension of other [purposes].
[The author asks: "But surely there is no 'having another purpose' at all for the Upaniṣadic statements; rather, they have as their purpose an already established fact (siddhārtha)."
Furthermore, since the understanding of its authority (*prāmāṇya*) depends upon its having a realized goal (*siddhārtha*), one might then say: "Let another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) be sought.

Or, if another means of knowledge does exist, what contradiction is there for us? The meaning of the scripture (*śāstra*) remains exactly as we have described it. But surely, if another means of knowledge exists, the meaning of the scripture is contradicted by [the existence of] difference (*bheda*).
Because it is being traversed. Indeed, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

If you consider there to be a contradiction, then there is no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) than this very contradiction itself. And apart from inference, unity cannot be asserted when there is a contradiction with scripture (āgama).

this is a specification of the agent (*kartṛnirdeśa*), not a specification of the entitlement (*adhikāranirdeśa*). Just as Brāhmaṇas and others are specified as agents in the fire-installation rites (*ādhāna*) performed at times such as spring, but not as those entitled [to them], so it is here as well. If that is the case, then—

Regarding the *ādhāna* (fire-laying) performed by them, who has the entitlement (*adhikāra*)? We say: none at all. Why, then, was it stated that the entitlement belongs to the three *varṇas*? It was stated that the entitlement to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices belongs to a member of the three *varṇas* who desires heaven. If that is so, then the *ādhāna* is merely a subsidiary (*aṅga*); it is not a primary act (*anaṅga*), because its purpose is for the sake of the fires. For the fires [are the means].

[The rites] have action as their purpose. How, then, can it be said that a member of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) who desires heaven is entitled (*adhikriyate*) to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices, given that the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is not an auxiliary (*anaṅga*) to them? For non-members of the three higher castes lack the sacred fires (*anagnitva*).
It has been stated that there is an entitlement (*adhikāra*). It is not the case that only those of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) are entitled;

thus, the entitlement to the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such sacrifices is indeed established. But as for the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), who is entitled? When it might initially be thought that everyone is entitled, [the conclusion is reached that] because of the lack of fulfillment of the caste-requisite (*jāty-aṅga*), it belongs only to those of the three higher castes. Just as in the case of one desiring sovereignty (*svārājya-kāma*), who is a Kṣatriya—

The entitlement for this very person is heard in the case of the Rājasūya; thus, it is established that it is exactly the same here as well. Furthermore, the entitlement to the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices should be understood as being based on the state of having maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgnitā*). As for those specific statements, however—

The *rāyovājīya* and other such [melodies] do not apply to this [fire-altar], yet they are not capable of setting aside its qualification (*adhikāra*). Furthermore, is it not the case that for the injunction of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), a qualification must be postulated just as it is for the *viśvajit* sacrifice? Let it be so; even then, there is no fault whatsoever. However, in this case, like the threshing (*āvadhāta*) and other [preparatory acts], there is no—
They maintain that this very injunction must be performed because it possesses a purpose; the rest has been explained.
