In this case as well, with respect to both learning and the performance of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) alone to be logical. For there may indeed be someone belonging to one of the three higher castes who is the master of the Niṣādas;
therefore, since there is no contradiction, he alone would have the entitlement [to the rite]. To this, it is replied: this is not a genitive compound.

Why? Because in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the word *niṣāda* functions with reference to the carpenter (*sthapati*) through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*); whereas in a descriptive compound (*karmadhāraya*), both words retain their own primary meanings. But is it not improper to say this, since the venerable Pāṇini, by the author of the Bhāṣya who justifies the option (*vāvacana*), has accepted that the sentence (*vākya*) and the compound (*vṛtti*) have the same meaning?

By whom was it stated that there is a multiplicity of meanings? Is it not the case that this was already stated—that the word *niṣāda* functions through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)? This is said with the acceptance of a specific purpose: here, the word *niṣāda* is employed in the sense of a carpenter (*sthapati*), and for him...

For in that case, the application [of the rule] is established through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). What does it indicate? It indicates the meaning of the genitive case. But if this is so, then the grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) of compounds with non-co-referential members (*vyadhikaraṇa-samāsa*) would be untenable; for the Blessed Pāṇini’s instruction proceeded for the purpose of restricting the expressive power of words in order to eliminate corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*). And under the view that secondary indication applies...
This is not a denotative word. For this very reason, Kātyāyana also stated that the mention of the particle *vā* is redundant.
Therefore, a distinction must be stated here. But is it not the case that this very distinction exists, since linguistic usage occurs even through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)?

In common usage, one observes such expressions as "a cowherd settlement dwells on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) and "the family of Garga [lives] by the well" (*kūpena gargakulam*). This application does not contradict the grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*), for the Blessed One’s instruction extends only as far as the word (*pada*).

And here, in its causal state (*nimittāvasthā*), this [word *gaṅgā*] is indeed expressive (*vācaka*); moreover, case-endings (*vibhakti*) are not restricted solely to those connected with what is directly expressive.

Thus he remembers; for because of the statement "from the nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*), he also remembers that while recollecting the rule "a grammatical operation concerning words applies when they are semantically connected" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*), case-endings arise from a semantically connected nominal stem.

Furthermore, apart from [the purpose of] efficacy and apart from the connection with its own meaning, there is therefore no established status as an "instruction" (*anuśāsana*). Nor is it a fixed rule for this teacher that instruction must have only the word (*pada*) as its limit;
it is also seen to have the sentence (*vākya*) as its limit, as in: "In the *kāṭhaka* [recension], [the substitution of *ī* and *ū* occurs] for *deva* and *sumna* in a *yajus*."
And because of the observation [in the Veda] that "the mother is the progenitor," the reason must be stated here for supporting the use of the particle *vā*.
This is now explained: this statement "or" (*vā*) is supported by accepting the operation of denotation (*abhidhāna*), not the operation of the object (*artha*).
And the object indicates another object, not denotation. But was it not said that the meaning of the genitive case is indicated?
For that very reason it was well said: for if the denotation were indicated by the genitive...

If this were said, there would be a fault. For it is not contradictory to accept that for some things the cause is the designation (*abhidhāna*), while for others it is the designated object (*abhihito ’rthaḥ*), because they have become such [by convention]. Indeed, [this does not contradict] the Blessed One’s...

This is a contradiction of the teaching. For grammar is indeed an instruction on linguistic usage (*prayoga*). There is no fault whatsoever in the fact that in some cases it is defined by its denotation (*abhidhāna*) and in others by its having the same meaning (*ekārthatā*). For this very reason, the author of the *Bhāṣya* says:
"Since usage depends upon us, why should we employ what is non-expressive (*avācaka*)?"
Thus. What is the intended meaning? This is the intended meaning: it is not proper to employ [a word] on the grounds that it lacks a denotation.

Who indeed perceives a distinction here? One perceives this: for when an effect has a single purpose, there is no beginninglessness to that effect. Since the effect depends upon this [designation], what else could it be than a verbal expression?
Therefore, it is well said that the Niṣāda alone is the *sthapati*. Thus, it is simply a matter of being based on verbal expression.
Thus ends the first quarter of the sixth chapter in the Bṛhatī.
The second quarter of the sixth chapter.
1. Since each [subsidiary act] serves to accomplish a single human purpose, there should be an entitlement to perform each one.
But surely, this was stated in the *Svargakāmādhikaraṇa*: "This number is not one pertaining to the qualified person (*adhikārin*);

rather, it is the number of the agent (*kartṛ*), because no other entity is mentioned. And so, how can there be a doubt as to whether a group (*pariṣad*) of those seeking [the result] has the qualification? It is said: in the subsequent section, regarding the verb...
The intended number of the agent will remain fixed. Once that number of the agent has been established,
does the qualification (adhikāra) correspond exactly to the agency, or is the agency one way while the qualification is another?

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that even in the case of the *adhikāra* (authorization/entitlement), the number residing in the agent is not capable of bringing about mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*). In this regard, the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) is as follows: because desire (*kāmanā*) is incompatible with the *adhikāra*, and because the attainment of the *adhikāra* occurs by way of agency (*kartṛtva*), and because the *adhikāra* is restricted to a single portion through the exclusion of others.

And since qualification (*adhikāra*) is determined by desire (*kāmitā*), it has been stated that the qualification belongs to the assembly (*pariṣad*) that desires [the result]. To this, it is replied: agency (*kartṛtva*) cannot restrict the attainment of the ritual act (*karmaprāpti*). We understand the attainment according to the verbal expression (*abhidhāna*), and not according to the connection with other word-meanings (*padārthāntara-saṃbandha*), such as the nominal stem *ṛddhikāma* (desiring prosperity).

Because it is something to be attained; and because its attainment and acquisition are connected with an agent. Furthermore, even agency here does not destroy independence, for while a plurality of agents is understood here, it is not a plurality of agencies.
What follows from this being so? This follows: there are many agents, but not many agencies; and therefore—

The coexistence here is verbal (*śābda*), not objective (*ārtha*). But surely, it is the state of being a joint agent (*saha-kartṛtva*) that is present here? The word *saha* here indicates objective coexistence. Why is this so? Precisely from the Bhāṣya itself: "of each one..."

When there is a desire to express independence (*svātantrya*), number is connected with the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). It is possible for each [agent] to have independence expressed; this understanding is logical because the case-endings (*vibhakti*) which occur cause one to understand that their referent is connected with number. And the meaning of the verbal suffix does not [express] number.

[The agent] partakes [of number]. Because it is not a real entity (*asattvabhūta*), therefore the *kārakas*—which are excluded [from being denoted by the verbal suffix] and are merely implied by it—partake of number. Since they are implied by the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) precisely in that state [of being non-real entities], they are not what is directly expressed by the word *kāraka*. On the other hand, nominal case-endings (*nāmavibhakti*) partake of number only with respect to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) itself; thus, [number] belongs only to that which resides therein.

[They] bring about a number. For this very reason, Agni and Soma [are the deities]; for deityhood is the state of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action), and in that state, the dual ending is produced from the nominal stems *agni* and *soma*.

The case ending does not express number; rather, it expresses [the number] only in the state of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). For this very reason, it is shown that while there is duality in the substratum, there is unity again in the status of the deity. Furthermore, since this number pertains to the originative injunction (*utpatti*), it must be understood as residing solely in the *kāraka* (grammatical participant). What is meant by "in the originative injunction"? It means it resides in the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).

The meaning is that the number does not pertain to the subordinate element (*upapada*). For if it pertained to the subordinate element, it would be understood as pertaining to the object (*karman*) as well, because it denotes [the agent] like a sentient being, as in the case of "he offers three oblations" (*tisra āhutīr juhoti*). Therefore, in this context, each one is understood to be independent;
for "the independent one is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*).

And because of such a traditional teaching (smṛti). Furthermore, plurality brings about a state of dependence on [other] agents; it does not mean that what is dependent possesses agency. Therefore, another agent is employed for the sake of achieving simultaneity (sāhitya), not for the sake of achieving agency itself. How, then, is there simultaneous denotation here? How?

And let there not be a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one); rather, there will be a simultaneous implication (*yugapadākṣepa*) of the subordinate terms (*upada*). Even if a *ekaśeṣa* is not possible without verbal expression, nevertheless, this alone is the intended meaning of the treatise. Therefore, just as—
Thus it is established that even when there is an agent, the assembly of petitioners has no entitlement [to the fruit].

2. Because the word "person" (puruṣa) is heard in the context of the performance, one may act according to one's desire regarding the performance. 3. One may act according to one's desire regarding the performance.

What is this statement that "the fruit of the treatise belongs to the agent"? What is its contradiction with that [previous position]? Or how is this obtained by it? When agency (*prayoktṛtva*) in the action is the meaning of the word, then the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) regarding the expression follows. When the expression is intended to be spoken, it is contradictory to claim that the denotation is unintended. Therefore, this was said:

"That very thing is being challenged. But how is it challenged? For regarding the action of one who is enjoined, the relationship is understood as "this belongs to him" or "he has this here. Therefore, the connection with number pertains only to one who has been enjoined.

Thus is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). It has been stated that the injunction (*niyoga*) pertains merely to the desire for a result and does not depend on number. Furthermore, it has been stated that the case-ending and number in the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāmaḥ*) are independent of the meaning of the verbal root. It has been explained that the connection of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) with the meaning of the verbal root constitutes his status as an agent (*kartṛtva*); the meaning is not that the injunction consists in the connection with the action itself.

Therefore, a number residing in an entity cannot be intended for expression, just like a number residing in a governing term (*adhikāra-pada*). Furthermore, it has been stated that this sentence extends as far as the fact that the fruit is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). And when the sentence is devoted to that [purpose], the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka-sambandha*) would all the more not be intended for expression. But surely, the relationship between action and its factors is also understood here?

How is it abandoned? Because the sentence has another purpose; for it has been stated that a single sentence has a single meaning. [Therefore, "one should eat poison" is not intended as a literal injunction. In this way, the illustration of the arrow-shooting becomes appropriate.
The indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been explained.
To this it is replied: neither the object (*karman*) nor the number can be said to be unintended (*avivakṣita*).
Why? Because eligibility (*adhikāra*) occurs only with respect to a qualified object. Just as [there is eligibility] for an action qualified by a substance—*p. 101*—so too...

Because it is understood from the context of entitlement (*adhikāra*), [the number] is not established by means of a separate substance; likewise, when the entitlement is understood with respect to an action qualified by the number of the agent, no other number is resorted to. Furthermore, that sentence does not have the sole purpose of stating "heaven belongs to the person"; rather, its meaning is "this person has entitlement to this action. And this is what constitutes entitlement.
Since it is understood that a specific action is prompted by its own result for the sake of the agent, everything is without fault.

And this being the case, it is also established that the result belongs to the prompter (*prayoktṛ*). For the prompter is indeed the qualified person (*adhikārin*). [The result belongs to] the agent—[p.
The third application for those who are destitute follows from this very point. Furthermore, as stated by the author of the Bhāṣya:

"Whether desiring heaven for oneself or for another, the designation 'one who desires heaven' (svargakāma) is indistinguishable; this is evident from the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) ending and from the indicative mark (*liṅga*), as well as from the mention of the agent using the middle voice in the context of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*). Thus, the fruits of the auxiliary rites are also [connected] to the principal."

The connection with the agent has been stated. What is expressed by this? All of this is obtained from the injunction (niyoga) as qualified by all its specific attributes: namely, that the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) makes known that the fruit belongs to the agent, and that the term *svargakāma* (desirer of heaven) denotes the state of desiring a desire connected to oneself. This very usage is also [the one] of Pāṇini.

The reason for mentioning the gender is that one remembers it thus: "the sacrificer sacrifices" (*yajate yajamānaḥ*) and "the priests sacrifice" (*yajanti yājakāḥ*). Therefore, since comprehension occurs exactly according to the cause, the author of the Bhāṣya provides this mention of the cause.
Thus, it is well said that the number is intended to be significant. As for the rule regarding each individual word (*pratipadvidhāna*), however...
It is displaced from its original context because it is impossible there;
however,
it should be restricted by the introductory sequence, since the commencement is governed by the ritual action.

But how, then, is there doubt here? Or how is there no doubt? It has been stated that the jurisdiction of desire (*kāmādhikāra*) extends up to the attainment of the fruit. In that regard, if desire ceases because the fruit has been attained through some other cause, or if that very jurisdiction ceases for some other reason, then for one who lacks such a jurisdiction, there can be no performance [of the rite].

Nor do we understand it from anything other than the word; therefore, we see this doubt as being entirely unfounded. It is said in reply: this is the gateway to the doubt here—those who know the qualification have stated that the connection between the action and so forth with the fruit and the person is preceded by "that which is to be done" (*kartavyatā*); for if one has engaged [in the act], one is impelled by that sense of "what ought to be done."

We understand this from the scripture (*śāstra*). And scripture is the expression of its own subject matter, beginning with the introduction and ending with the final liberation (*apavarga*). Therefore, it does not remain incomplete, because the meaning of the injunction (*niyoga*) is not understood part by part.

But surely, in that case, it has been stated that the fact that ritual action exists for the sake of a fruit is not tenable. First, as a cause for engagement [in action], this is not untenable; and it has been stated that the scripture is the instrument (*karaṇa*) precisely because the engagement is not yet completed. Beyond this, where would the persistence of the qualification (*adhikāra*) be of use? Therefore, even when the desire for a fruit has ceased, [the engagement continues] until completion.
[The opponent] considers that action is the primary thing.
This being the case, it is replied: It is true that the purpose of the scripture extends up to liberation (*apavarga*);

and it is true that [the meaning] is not understood through its constituent parts alone. However, one cannot understand that the scripture is the cause [of knowledge] apart from its specific subject matter (*adhikāra*).

It is possible. But has it not been stated that the performance of the rite is logically established as the occasion for action? A non-accomplished thing cannot serve as an occasion; for an occasion is precisely that which is already apprehended, not one that is yet to be accomplished.

It has been stated that [an action] is understood by way of its cause (*nimitta*). Therefore, even in the case of engagement, experts in logic maintain that engagement occurs only so long as there is a cause, and its cessation is logical when the cause is absent. Furthermore, as for that which was said by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*)—namely, "I must do this"—it refers to the means (*upāya*).
"But one does not know [it]"; this is the meaning: when the desire for the fruit has ceased, the scripture is no longer directly manifest.

Therefore, once the desire for the fruit has vanished and the meaning of the scripture has been ascertained, it is not possible for the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) to function as the cause.
And since entitlement (*adhikāra*) consists in that which serves as the cause, it is precisely this absence of the scriptural meaning that has been demonstrated.

[Page 106] But is this not in contradiction with the *bhāvārtha-adhikaraṇa*? It has been shown in the *svargakāma-adhikaraṇa* how it is not contradictory. Furthermore, as for this presentation of an alternative view, it is because it is censured by the learned (*śiṣṭa*).

"It must be brought to completion. To the question "Why so?", [the author] responds by raising an objection: "They censure it. He then states that this very censure by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) is the reason for the completion [of the act], without requiring any other cause, and he demonstrates the fault of false resolve (*mithyā-saṅkalpa*). This appears somewhat inconsistent. How is it inconsistent? If...

[Objection: In that case, the commencement and completion [of the work] would be impossible for the very purpose of avoiding the fault of false resolve (*mithyā-saṅkalpa*), so why is the introduction of the censure of the learned (*viśiṣṭa-vigarhaṇā*) presented here? [Response: It is said in reply: There is no such thing as "false resolve" in this context at all. For the resolve made here is directed toward the subject matter of the treatise (*śāstrārtha*). Moreover, the completion [of the work] by one who desires to discern [the truth] is not the subject matter of the treatise. As for those who censure [the author]—

The remaining [opponents] think as follows: "He has the fault of false resolve, in that he does not bring what has been commenced to completion"; thinking thus, they censure him. Therefore, because of that censure, one must complete it.
Why do they resort to a baseless censure? What is the use of searching for its foundation here? This very [censure]—
For [it] is indeed the cause of suffering; and since those who are skillful exert effort in avoiding the causes of suffering, it is well said that "the learned first of all censure [it]."
In this world, ritual actions are like the Vedas; from them arises knowledge of the Supreme Person.

Regarding the work performed by those who hold the scriptures, such as the construction of houses and the like: should that which has been commenced be brought to completion, or should one desist from it once the desire for the fruit has vanished? Now, one might argue that because of the fear of being censured by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), the action must be completed; however, this [obligation] is not scriptural (*śāstrīya*). Therefore, it is precisely that [scriptural principle] which should be followed here. What, then, do they censure?

"No," [it may be objected]. "What is the point of following whether something is scriptural or non-scriptural? It is said in reply: This is true indeed, provided that the censure of it is unconditional. However, they censure it because it is scriptural, not because it is non-scriptural. Therefore, it must be investigated in order to dispel various misconceptions regarding it; for in this matter, there is a connection with the deity.

The prima facie position is that it is scriptural because of the prescription of expiatory rites; for that which is non-scriptural cannot have a scriptural element as its constituent part, nor can there be a rectification of its deficiency through such means.

To this it is replied: there is no authoritative evidence that [the assignment of houses and so forth] is not scriptural, because the effort [involved] has a pleasant purpose. Furthermore, as for what the authors of the Sūtras record—namely, "this house belongs to the Brāhmaṇa," "this belongs to the King"—and how they record that there is a transgression such as death if one acts otherwise than what was enjoined, even that [applies only to matters such as] medicine and the like.

This is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). As for the fact that there are expiations (*prāyaścitta*) and prescriptions regarding deities (*devatā-vidhāna*), these have been refuted on the grounds that they serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) and are not for the sake of acts such as house-building.
In the case of prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*), since there is no [independent] action, there would be an act consisting of the performance of what is prohibited.
Because actions are divided [into different classes]. || 17 ||

What is this deliberation regarding the operation of the injunction (*niyoga*): is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) that is enjoined, or is it the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), or that which is qualified by it? This is a deliberation concerning the second alternative, the injunction. What is the fault? Indeed, there is none.
There is no fault; however, there is a lack of connection regarding the definition of qualification (*adhikāra*). If that is so, then this is merely an inquiry into qualification.

How is there an inquiry into qualification? In this way: if the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is enjoined here, then the verb *bhakṣayati* (he eats) becomes a qualifier of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*). Therefore, it is an injunction of an action qualified by the meaning of the negative particle. From that, [the rest] is to be inferred...

[The qualification of] the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) is like that of the Viśvajit sacrifice; and for the sake of establishing that, this consideration of relative strength (*balābala*) has been introduced. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), holding the general rule (*utsarga*) that "verbs denote the meaning of the action" (*bhāvārthāḥ karmaśabdāḥ*), considers it to be a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) because the injunction of the subordinate term (*upapada*) is dependent upon that [action]. Furthermore, regarding the injunction of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*):

It follows that there must be performance [of such an act]. How so? For even that which is prohibited, if it does not benefit a person—either by way of prosperity (*abhyudaya*) or by the removal of suffering (*duḥkhaparihāra*)—people who act with deliberation do not engage in it; this is what worldly people say.

Therefore, this alone is the superior meaning of the sentence. [Objection: But even if there is an injunction regarding the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), let there be the postulation of demerit (*pratyavāya*). [Reply: How can demerit be postulated when there is an injunction of the meaning of the negative particle? Furthermore, performance would not even be possible. If it is argued that demerit is postulated through the performance of the [prohibited] object, then that [demerit] must arise from the performance of the prohibition itself.

"It is avoided as if it were worldly"—this is incorrect. For the injunction regarding the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) does not terminate in that meaning alone; rather, the performance of the action is what pertains to the world.
And if no transgression is understood from a worldly performance, how could it be understood from anything else?

Therefore, human purpose cannot be established otherwise; thus, there must be an injunction against eating. To this, it is replied: True, as the "Beloved of the Gods" (the Fools) has said; however, this is not understood to be an injunction against eating. For the verb *bhakṣayati* denotes the act of eating, while the negative particle (*nañ*) denotes prohibition.

[He] states [the meaning of] cessation. Even by the two words, only non-eating is understood as something unreal; and that cannot be enjoined because it is not of the nature of an action. However, a mental operation [is not derived] from the word, nor from the sentence.

It is understood that in the case of "not looking" (*anīkṣaṇa*) and so forth, the word *vrata* (vow) is heard directly [in the scripture]. Therefore, the root *bhakṣayati* (to eat) is a qualification of the person qualified (*adhikṛta-viśeṣaṇa*), and it is simply improper to treat the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*)—that is, the state of non-existence or indifference—as something to be enjoined. Now, it was argued that performance would not be possible; why is it not possible?

Does it follow that there is no comprehension of what ought to be done? For it has been demonstrated in the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* that desires and the like are connected only when there is a comprehension of what ought to be done. Where those [agents], such as those desiring heaven, exist, there alone does the comprehension of what ought to be done extend up to the attainment of prosperity (*abhyudaya*). But where they do not exist, what [comprehension] could there be?

[The opponent] denies the comprehension of what is to be done (*kartavyatāvagama*). However, it has been stated that performance follows from the comprehension of what is to be done, and not from the comprehension of the result, because the comprehension of the result is rooted in that [comprehension of what is to be done]. For this very reason, even [the desire for] livelihood and so forth—

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that because it is impossible for [the Self] to function as a qualification and because there is no specific qualified person (*adhikārī*), a qualification must be supplied by implication (*adhyāhārya*), just as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others. What is the reasoning?

It is not possible for an unestablished entity to serve as a qualification of a qualified person. Why? Because [an entity] must be either something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) or already established (*siddha*) in order to be considered "pertaining to the next world" (*pāralaukika*).

It is connected. What follows from that? This results: it is connected by way of being an established means of accomplishment (*siddha-niṣpādakatayā*); the goal (*sādhya*) is connected by way of being the fruit (*phalatayā*). Life is established [as the occasion for action]. Therefore, he considers that its status as a means (*sādhanabhāva*) alone is logical. However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that the observation of the debt (*ṛṇadarśana*) indicates the necessity of performance; life constitutes the qualification (*adhikāra*).

It makes known [the agent] by way of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatayā*). Now, one might object: "Since a relationship is not possible for an established entity apart from its status as a means to an end (*sādhanabhāva*), what will the vision [of the Veda] accomplish here? To this it is replied: We have already stated in the *Svargakāmādhikaraṇa* that the mandate (*niyoga*) does not belong to the agent (*kartṛ*). And it has been said that the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) exists only so long as there is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) indicated by the word.

Therefore, being the object to be accomplished (*sādhyatā*) is not the reason for [the injunction] being a qualification of the person prompted (*niyojya*). And it has been stated that the qualification of the person prompted is the qualification of the entitled agent (*adhikārin*). Furthermore, the consistency of the scriptural observation regarding debts would otherwise be untenable.

Thus it has been stated. Therefore, it is established that these rites are indeed obligatory because their occasion is obligatory. Alternatively, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) maintains that only the Brāhmaṇa has the entitlement [to perform these rites], since the word "Brāhmaṇa" is heard in the statement regarding the debts (*ṛṇavākya*), and thus these rites belong to the Brāhmaṇa alone; for the word "Brāhmaṇa" is not heard in the actual injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*).
